question: Why is it important to keep hospital bed sheets smooth and tight?

options.A: To help the mattress last longer over time
options.B: To make the hospital room look neat for visitors
options.C: To prevent skin breakdown and pressure sores
options.D: To reduce the overall workload of the ward cleaners

explanation: You're doing great! Wrinkles and creases press hard against fragile skin, which can quickly cause painful pressure sores. Keeping sheets smooth keeps our patients safe and comfortable. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T2#GNS112_U4_T2_h1)

question: As a student nurse, why should you view bed making as a key clinical task rather than just simple cleaning?

options.A: Because patients cannot sleep without nurse assistance
options.B: Because doctors evaluate nurses based on sheet folding
options.C: Because hospital management requires strict cleaning logs
options.D: Because it directly supports patient recovery and comfort

explanation: Spot on! Bed making isn't just about tidiness—it directly protects your patient's skin, helps them rest better, and aids their overall healing journey. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T2#GNS112_U4_T2_h1)

question: Why must you always hold soiled bed linen away from your uniform?

options.A: To make it easier to carry heavy bundles of sheets
options.B: To keep the uniform from getting wrinkled on duty
options.C: To comply with laundry room sorting regulations
options.D: To prevent the transfer of microorganisms to clothing

explanation: Good nursing habit! Keeping dirty sheets away from your scrubs stops germs from hitching a ride onto your clothes and spreading to the next patient. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T2#GNS112_U4_T2_h2)

question: When clearing a hospital bed, which action should you definitely avoid?

options.A: Washing hands after handling the items
options.B: Folding the linen into a compact bundle
options.C: Shaking the linen in the air
options.D: Placing the linen straight into a hamper

explanation: Never shake dirty sheets! Shaking sends dust, skin flakes, and germs flying into the air where everyone in the ward can breathe them in. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T2#GNS112_U4_T2_h2)

question: What is the main job of a draw sheet on a hospital bed?

options.A: To serve as an extra blanket during cold nights
options.B: To replace the pillowcase when extra support is needed
options.C: To cover the patient's face during minor examinations
options.D: To help lift and reposition patients in bed easily

explanation: You've got this! A draw sheet is a lifesaver—it lets you slide or lift patients smoothly without dragging their skin and causing friction burns. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T2#GNS112_U4_T2_h3)

question: What should you do with clean extra linen that you brought into an isolation room but didn't end up using?

options.A: Give the extra items to a patient in the next ward
options.B: Treat it as contaminated and send it to the laundry
options.C: Return it immediately to the central linen storage
options.D: Store it in the patient's bedside locker for later

explanation: Safety first! Once clean linen enters an isolation room, it's considered exposed to germs and must go to the laundry, never back to clean stock. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T2#GNS112_U4_T2_h3)

question: When do you normally make an unoccupied bed in the ward?

options.A: Whenever the patient complains of feeling too hot
options.C: When the patient is ambulant, bathing, or discharged
options.D: Only during the morning shift before the doctor's visit

explanation: Easy peasy! An unoccupied bed is made when the bed is empty, such as when a patient is up walking around, bathing, or has been discharged. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T2#GNS112_U4_T2_h4)

question: Why do nurses finish one entire side of an unoccupied bed before walking over to do the other side?

options.A: To keep the pillows from falling onto the ward floor
options.B: To ensure the top sheet is always placed before the blanket
options.C: To maximize physical efficiency and reduce unnecessary walking
options.D: To prevent the mattress from sliding off the metal frame

explanation: Smart nursing saves energy! Working methodically on one side lets you tuck everything in completely before making just one trip to the other side. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T2#GNS112_U4_T2_h4)

question: Before turning a patient to make an occupied bed, what vital safety step must you take on the far side of the bed?

options.D: Lower the bed to the floor

explanation: Patient safety is everything! Always raise the side rails on the opposite side first so the patient is protected from accidentally rolling out. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T2#GNS112_U4_T2_h5)

question: During an occupied bed procedure, how do you handle the soiled bottom sheet?

options.A: Rolled close to the patient's back before being tucked under
options.B: Lifted over the patient's head to reach the laundry hamper
options.C: Cut into smaller pieces to make removal easier
options.D: Pulled quickly from underneath the patient in one sharp movement

explanation: Brilliant! Rolling the dirty sheet neatly right against the patient's back clears space to roll out and tuck in the clean sheet smoothly. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T2#GNS112_U4_T2_h5)

question: Where should you leave the call bell after you finish making an occupied bed?

options.A: Within easy reach of the patient's hand
options.B: On top of the bedside table out of reach
options.C: Inside the bottom drawer of the locker
options.D: Hanging from the footboard near the IV pole

explanation: Always make sure the call bell is right by the patient's hand before you leave, so they can easily call for help whenever they need it. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T2#GNS112_U4_T2_h6)

question: What is the main reason to note any skin changes you spot while making a patient's bed?

options.A: To prove to the hospital administration that linens were changed
options.B: To satisfy the laundry department's daily record requirements
options.C: To help the doctor prescribe stronger pain medications
options.D: To monitor for early signs of pressure sores and track changes

explanation: You've got this! Bed making puts you up close with the patient's skin, making it the perfect chance to catch early redness or breakdown. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T2#GNS112_U4_T2_h6)
